edition.deck: A US aviation shutdown exposes ageing infrastructure; fresh diplomatic, security and public-service developments shape the day.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises overnight developments and substantial new information. Returning stories are included only where the gather records a meaningful update; repeated coverage without a fresh development is omitted.

content.headline: US lifts nationwide flight stop after air traffic control communications failure
content.shortHeadline: US reopens skies after nationwide air traffic control failure
content.standfirst: A communications breakdown grounded US departures for more than four hours, delaying and cancelling thousands of flights. Officials say ageing equipment failed, with no indication of a cyberattack; the cause remains under investigation.

image.caption: Travellers wait at John F Kennedy International Airport during the US flight disruption.

sources.originalTitle: What we know about the longest US nationwide flight ground stop since 9/11
US aviation agency lifts nationwide ground stop affecting all air travel
‘It’s frustrating’: chaos at US airports as stoppage grinds travel plans to a halt

segments.body: The Federal Aviation Administration lifted its nationwide ground stop after a communications failure affected air traffic control centres. The shutdown lasted more than four hours. FlightAware figures cited by the BBC showed more than 8,500 delays and nearly 8,000 cancellations; figures reported by The Guardian differed, reflecting separate tallies.

segments.title: Ageing system under scrutiny
segments.body: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said an old communications system became overloaded after new technology was introduced, affecting communications and radar. He estimated a complete overhaul could cost $50bn. Officials said they had seen no evidence of an attack and that the public was not in danger. The Guardian reported that the White House and FAA also asked Congress for further modernisation funding.

content.headline: White House says Trump, Putin and Xi plan unprecedented meeting in China
content.shortHeadline: Trump, Putin and Xi plan meeting at China summit
content.standfirst: The White House says the three leaders intend to meet on the sidelines of next week’s Apec summit. Moscow and Beijing have not confirmed the plan, and US officials do not expect an agreement to follow.

image.caption: Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet in Washington in September.

sources.originalTitle: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
Trump deltager torsdag i historisk møde med Putin og Xi

segments.body: White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping plan a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen during the Apec summit. It would be the first such meeting of the three leaders, according to reporting in the gather. China’s state media has referred to Xi’s bilateral talks, while Moscow and Beijing have not confirmed the proposed three-way meeting.

segments.title: Nuclear arms on the agenda
segments.body: Wales said Trump intends to discuss reducing nuclear weapons. A US official cited by news agencies said no agreement was expected. The meeting would come after the US-Russia nuclear arms control treaty expired in February, leaving their arsenals without major treaty limits, and amid Trump’s stated interest in a broader agreement involving China.

content.headline: Ukraine reports Starshield limits as Russian strikes hit cities and hospital
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine says Starshield limits hamper defences as Russia strikes
content.standfirst: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says speed restrictions remain along the front line, complicating drone interceptions. Russian attacks caused casualties in several Ukrainian cities, as the shape of future peace talks remains disputed.

image.caption: Ukrainian soldiers move through an area exposed to Russian drone attacks.

sources.originalTitle: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says Starshield restrictions continue on ‘entire front line’
The move that shows Putin has Trump’s backing in Ukraine pressure campaign
Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine

segments.body: Zelenskyy said restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield satellite communications remained in place along the front line and in occupied areas, making it harder to intercept jet-powered drones. Russia struck Kyiv’s National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedics, injuring three people, according to The Guardian; other Russian attacks killed people and injured dozens in Zaporizhzhia and Odesa, regional officials said.

segments.title: Dispute over who joins talks
segments.body: Ukraine and US envoys have discussed European participation in future negotiations, but the Kremlin said no decision had been made. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that Russia’s push to discuss Europe’s wider security arrangements could distract from securing a ceasefire. BBC Russia editor Steve Rosenberg writes that Moscow views the return of its 2021 security proposals to the discussions as a political gain.

perspectives.body: BBC Russia editor Steve Rosenberg says the Kremlin’s renewed push to reshape European security echoes demands rejected by Western governments in 2021, shortly before Russia launched its full-scale invasion.

content.headline: Microsoft says services fully restored after global outage
content.shortHeadline: Microsoft says global outage is over as services return
content.standfirst: Microsoft said early Saturday that services affected by the outage had been restored, after disruption lasting more than a day. The company has apologised; a fuller account of what went wrong is still to come.

image.caption: Microsoft Teams and Outlook were among the services disrupted by the outage.

sources.originalTitle: Alle Microsofts tjenester virker igen efter globalt nedbrud
Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage as it reports broad recovery
Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
How Microsoft outage has affected key public services in the UK

segments.body: Microsoft said Teams, Outlook, Copilot and other affected services were functioning normally again early Saturday, Danish time, according to DR. The outage disrupted digital communications for businesses and public agencies in more than 70 countries. Microsoft says more than 430 million people use the affected Microsoft 365 products.

segments.title: Impact and cause still under review
segments.body: The disruption affected organisations including parts of the UK health service, schools and police forces, as well as businesses and government agencies elsewhere. Microsoft attributed the failure to a technical issue during a network capacity upgrade, not a cyberattack, and said it would publish a post-incident review once its investigation is complete.

content.headline: Megaspeed investigation puts Singapore’s role in chip trade under scrutiny
content.shortHeadline: Megaspeed probe tests Singapore’s role in global chip trade
content.standfirst: Singapore is investigating whether companies made false declarations about servers bought and exported through the city-state, amid suspicions that restricted Nvidia chips reached China. The company denies wrongdoing; investigations continue.

image.caption: Singapore, a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips.

sources.originalTitle: How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
Pressure grows on Trump's Commerce Secretary Lutnick in fallout from Nvidia scandal

segments.body: Singapore said it has investigated whether Megaspeed and other firms falsely declared the destinations of data servers bought and exported through the city-state. Authorities suspect the equipment may have gone elsewhere than the neighbouring Malaysia named in company declarations. Singapore says it found insufficient evidence of a crime by Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, and has yet to charge the company or people linked to the case. Investigations by Singapore and the US are ongoing.

segments.title: Export controls and political pressure
segments.body: The case spotlights Singapore’s role as a major ordering hub for Nvidia chips: the BBC reported that less than 1% of Nvidia’s Singapore billings last year were for chips that entered the country. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said several agencies had supported putting Megaspeed on an export-control list months earlier, pointing to the Commerce Department’s authority. Congressional scrutiny is also growing over possible chip diversion and Nvidia’s oversight of customers.

perspectives.body: Bessent’s public criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick brings an internal dispute over export controls into view. Bessent also questioned whether Nvidia had done enough to prevent chips reaching pass-through companies.

content.headline: Uganda succession tensions deepen as army arrests and threats fuel speculation
content.shortHeadline: Uganda succession tensions grow amid military arrests and threats
content.standfirst: Army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the president’s son, has threatened the vice-president as arrests of senior officers fuel debate over who will succeed Yoweri Museveni. The military cites anti-corruption work; critics suspect political motives.

image.caption: Ugandan army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba has signalled interest in the presidency.

sources.originalTitle: Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever

segments.body: At least a dozen Ugandan generals and senior officers have been arrested since April 2025, according to the Daily Monitor investigation cited by the BBC. The latest tensions include army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba’s threats against Vice-President Jessica Alupo, whom he said should prepare to hand over her office. Alupo remains in post and has not publicly responded.

segments.title: Competing explanations
segments.body: The military describes the arrests as efforts to address corruption and criminality. Political scientist Gerald Bareebe argues that officers seen as opposed to Kainerugaba’s possible succession are being targeted; security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations across security agencies. The ruling party has rejected reports that it decided against backing Kainerugaba, and the government has dismissed claims of a succession fallout.

content.headline: AI helps decode Gödel notebooks, yielding hundreds of mathematical results
content.shortHeadline: AI helps decode Gödel notebooks, revealing hundreds of results
content.standfirst: A researcher says AI helped him analyse dense, shorthand-filled notebooks by the logician Kurt Gödel. Some of the reconstructed results have been checked with proof software, but their interpretation and historical significance remain under discussion.

image.caption: Kurt Gödel’s work influenced modern logic and the development of computation.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths

segments.body: Finnish logician Jan von Plato used the AI model Claude to help analyse 1,009 pages of Gödel’s notebooks, much of them written in obsolete German shorthand. He says Claude identified 663 theorems for which Gödel had proved, sketched or proposed a proof. When checked with the proof assistant Coq, about 400 were verified as stated, about 200 needed repairs and about 50 were false.

segments.title: What the notebooks establish
segments.body: Von Plato says the notebooks contain results that anticipate later work and themes in logic that have drawn little attention. But mathematician Joel David Hamkins, who has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of a proof, cautions that resemblance to a later result does not establish that Gödel had completed it. The distinction between Gödel’s work and the AI’s contribution remains for researchers to assess.

perspectives.body: University of Notre Dame logician Joel David Hamkins says that although the notebooks may contain exciting ideas, determining how much belongs to Gödel and how much to Claude requires further historical and mathematical scrutiny.

content.headline: SpaceX aborts Starship booster catch during test flight
content.shortHeadline: SpaceX diverts Starship booster after catch attempt is aborted
content.standfirst: The Super Heavy booster was diverted to the ocean rather than caught by the launch tower’s mechanical arms. The upper stage continued its test flight, with SpaceX assessing whether it can attempt a return later on Saturday.

image.caption: The Super Heavy booster was diverted to the ocean after its attempted catch was aborted.

sources.originalTitle: Setback for SpaceX Starship rocket's double-catch test
SpaceX opgiver at indfange løfteraket efter Starship-opsendelse

segments.body: SpaceX aborted an attempt to catch the Super Heavy booster after Starship launched from Texas. The booster was diverted to the ocean and broke up as it came down. The company has not explained why the catch was called off; DR reported a SpaceX spokesman saying the reason was not yet known.

segments.title: A high-stakes test
segments.body: The upper stage, called Ship, continued its flight and was due to complete 14 orbits before a possible return to the launch tower later on Saturday. SpaceX’s aim is to recover both stages so the rocket can be reused. The company’s progress matters to NASA’s plans for a lunar lander, although the gather notes that the programme is already running behind its intended pace.

content.headline: Probation officers vote for strike action over pay and workloads
content.shortHeadline: Probation officers vote to strike over pay and workloads
content.standfirst: The union Napo says action is likely to begin with overtime restrictions on 23 November, with strikes planned later. The dispute adds pressure to a service monitoring offenders released early to relieve prison overcrowding.

image.caption: Probation officers monitor offenders and oversee their rehabilitation in the community.

sources.originalTitle: Probation officers in England and Wales vote to strike over pay and workloads

segments.body: Probation officers in England and Wales voted in favour of strike action and other measures over a 5% pay offer and workloads, the union Napo said. Overtime restrictions are expected to start on 23 November, with strikes to follow at a later stage. The union had sought a 12% increase.

segments.title: Pressure on supervision
segments.body: Probation staff monitor offenders’ behaviour, rehabilitation and electronic tags, and can recall people to prison for breaches. Around 2,500 offenders, including sex offenders and domestic abusers, are expected to be released under the current early-release scheme by the end of the year. The Ministry of Justice says it is recruiting 1,300 trainee officers and has contingency plans to maintain supervision.

content.headline: US Air Force responds to suspected drone activity at RAF Lakenheath
content.shortHeadline: Suspected drone activity reported at RAF Lakenheath
content.standfirst: The US Air Force says security personnel responded to suspected unauthorised drone activity at the Suffolk base on Friday night. It reported no effect on people, aircraft or infrastructure and said the situation was resolved.

image.caption: The main entrance to RAF Lakenheath, a US military airbase in Suffolk.

sources.originalTitle: US Air Force responds to suspected drone activity at RAF Lakenheath

segments.body: The US Air Force said it responded to suspected unauthorised drone activity at RAF Lakenheath on Friday night. No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, and the situation was resolved, according to the force and the UK Ministry of Defence. Authorities said they were working to establish the facts.

segments.title: Security context
segments.body: The base is home to the US Air Force’s 48th Fighter Wing. The MP for West Suffolk said authorities had told him there was no threat to the public. The incident comes amid wider concern about security at US military sites in Britain, but the gather does not establish who was responsible or whether any drone was confirmed.

content.headline: Letters show Reform’s Richard Tice urged Bank of England to ease crypto rules
content.shortHeadline: Letters show Tice pressed Bank for lighter crypto rules
content.standfirst: Private correspondence shows Reform UK’s deputy leader called for a “light touch” approach to stablecoins after the party received a £9m donation from crypto investor Christopher Harborne. The report says there is no evidence Harborne asked Tice to lobby.

image.caption: Richard Tice is Reform UK’s deputy leader and its business, trade and energy spokesperson.

sources.originalTitle: Reform deputy leader Richard Tice lobbied Bank of England on crypto after £9m donation

segments.body: Letters released by the Bank of England show Richard Tice pressed officials in November and December 2025 to loosen the approach to stablecoin regulation. He argued that the UK risked losing business to the US and described Reform UK as being “set to form the next government”. The correspondence came four months after the party received a £9m donation from cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne.

segments.title: No evidence of donor request
segments.body: The i Paper reports no suggestion that Harborne asked Tice to write to the Bank or that Tice acted on his behalf. Tice says his intervention reflects his longstanding support for financial deregulation. Reform has denied that its donors expect anything in return for their contributions.

content.headline: Campaigners urge Xi summit invitation to depend on lifting UK sanctions
content.shortHeadline: Campaigners say Xi visit should depend on lifting UK sanctions
content.standfirst: Critics want China to lift sanctions on British politicians and others before President Xi is invited to next year’s G20 in Manchester. Their demand follows reports of an effort to obtain personal information about some of those sanctioned; an FBI investigation is ongoing.

image.caption: Xi Jinping at the G20 summit in Rio de Janeiro in 2024.

sources.originalTitle: The new China spy scandal that’s sparking fury at proposed Xi UK visit

segments.body: Former Conservative minister Iain Duncan Smith and other campaigners have urged the government to make any invitation to Xi Jinping conditional on China lifting sanctions imposed on British citizens and MPs. The restrictions, imposed in 2021, bar those targeted from travelling to China and Chinese organisations from doing business with them. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is keen to welcome Xi to the G20 in Manchester in 2027.

segments.title: Allegations remain under investigation
segments.body: The renewed dispute follows a report that people allegedly acting for Chinese interests sought personal and financial information about sanctioned MPs. Security Minister Dan Jarvis confirmed an FBI investigation was ongoing and that there was a live Interpol arrest warrant, but declined to discuss the specific allegations. The Foreign Office is seeking clarification from Beijing about the sanctions.

content.headline: UK and EU plan medicine-supply agreement amid shortages
content.shortHeadline: UK and EU plan deal to share medicine shortage information
content.standfirst: A proposed health-security agreement would let Britain and the EU share information about medicine shortages and ways to find supplies. It is expected to be part of the reset package discussed at next week’s summit, not yet a signed deal.

image.caption: Antibiotic tablets on a pharmaceutical production line.

sources.originalTitle: Pharmacies to have better access to antibiotics and ADHD drugs in new Brexit deal

segments.body: A draft UK-EU statement refers to a memorandum of understanding on health security at the 20 November summit. The proposed arrangement would help the two sides alert one another to shortages and share information on sourcing medicines. Experts quoted by The i Paper called it a significant first step, but the agreement is still being negotiated.

segments.title: Shortages affect multiple treatments
segments.body: The gather cites shortages affecting antibiotics, ADHD and epilepsy medicines, as well as Creon, used by some people with cystic fibrosis and pancreatic conditions. Nuffield Trust researcher Mark Dayan says earlier information could help officials identify where stocks are available and reduce the risk that shortages reach patients. The report also notes that post-Brexit trade barriers add to the UK’s supply challenges.

content.headline: Ministers consider marketplace restrictions amid child-safety concerns
content.shortHeadline: UK considers marketplace age limits over child-safety fears
content.standfirst: Ministers are considering whether to restrict under-16s’ access to online marketplaces after reports of sexualised messages and manipulated images. Child-safety campaigners warn a broad ban may not make platforms safer by design.

image.caption: Children’s secondhand clothing listings can attract sexualised messages on resale platforms.

sources.originalTitle: The dark side of reselling apps: ‘If you include your pants, I’ll pay more’

segments.body: The government is considering extending possible age restrictions to online marketplaces such as Depop, eBay and Facebook Marketplace, according to the report. Children’s clothing listings have attracted sexualised messages, and one young seller said images of her were taken from resale sites and later altered into explicit deepfakes. Vinted says its minimum age is 18; Depop allows users aged 13 and over, subject to payment restrictions.

segments.title: Safeguards and trade-offs
segments.body: The Children’s Society says some young users have been asked for explicit images in exchange for money or gifts. Ministers are weighing restrictions, but a charity supporting victims of technology-assisted abuse cautions that a broad ban may not be the best solution compared with making platforms safer by design. One seller said she worried restrictions could remove a source of money for girls from less well-off backgrounds.

content.headline: Calls grow for stronger protection of 16- and 17-year-olds from exploitation
content.shortHeadline: Calls grow for stronger protection of 16- and 17-year-olds
content.standfirst: Campaigners and some Labour MPs want the law to account for age gaps and power imbalances in sexual relationships involving 16- and 17-year-olds. Researchers caution that changing the law alone may not prevent grooming and could create new barriers to support.

image.caption: David Walliams has denied allegations made against him by multiple women.

sources.originalTitle: Walliams allegations prompt calls for staggered age of consent at 16 and 17

segments.body: The allegations reported against Russell Brand and David Walliams have prompted renewed calls for greater legal protection for 16- and 17-year-olds from exploitation by much older adults. The Close the Consent Gap campaign proposes making sexual activity with a 16- or 17-year-old a criminal offence when the other person is more than three years older. The proposal is not current law.

segments.title: Debate over effects
segments.body: Victims’ commissioner Claire Waxman has called for serious discussion of legislative change. Barrister Charlotte Proudman says a graduated age of consent would recognise age and power differences. Researchers quoted in the report question the evidence that such a change would work and warn it could deter young people from seeking advice or support.

content.headline: HS2 tunnel sealed again as major works lag behind schedule
content.shortHeadline: HS2 tunnel sealed as construction remains years behind
content.standfirst: The completed Long Itchington Wood tunnel has been sealed while the rest of the civil works catch up. HS2’s chief executive says track-laying is not expected to begin until 2030, with the first section now forecast to open between 2036 and 2039.

image.caption: The Long Itchington Wood tunnel was the first tunnel completed for HS2.

sources.originalTitle: HS2 celebrated finishing its first tunnel… then months later sealed it back up

segments.body: Contractors have resealed the one-mile Long Itchington Wood tunnel in Warwickshire, a year after it was hailed as the first completed tunnel on HS2. The project’s chief executive, Mark Wild, says the civil engineering phase is about 70% complete and that the first track is not expected to be laid until 2030.

segments.title: Cost, pace and disagreement
segments.body: The government confirmed in May that the 140-mile London-to-Birmingham line is expected to cost more than £100bn; it says £43.6bn had been spent by February 2026. A rail campaigner and engineer quoted by The i Paper argue that spending constraints are holding up work. Wild says delivery coordination, not money, is the constraint, and warns against speeding up by taking “crazy risks”.

content.headline: Danish navy plan leak prompts internal inquiry and criticism
content.shortHeadline: Navy plan leak sparks inquiry and criticism of defence command
content.standfirst: An internal Danish Navy document calls for a hybrid fleet, including frigates, drones and smaller combat ships. After DR reported its contents, the Defence Command said it would investigate who shared the document; a retired colonel criticised that response.

image.caption: A Danish frigate at sea, part of the navy’s current fleet.

sources.originalTitle: Hemmeligt notat viser Søværnets plan for fremtidens flåde - og der er brug for meget mere end nye fregatter
Forsvaret vil efterforske læk af hemmelig flådeplan til DR

segments.body: A Danish Navy internal document describes a proposed “hybrid fleet” built around frigates, with drones operating above, on and beneath the water, and a new type of smaller combat ship. The document says six frigates would be needed to meet NATO force targets; DR reports that Denmark currently has five. The navy’s proposals are not a final government decision.

segments.title: Response to the disclosure
segments.body: After DR reported the document, the Defence Command said the information did not represent the armed forces’ recommendations for the future fleet and reported the disclosure to the military prosecution service. Retired colonel Eigil Schjønning criticised the inquiry, saying the document was internal but not classified. A defence-policy researcher said the investigation reflected a desire to keep documents within their intended circles.

perspectives.body: Retired colonel Eigil Schjønning argues that once the document was public, the armed forces should have addressed its substance rather than focusing on who disclosed it. He fears the navy’s operational needs might otherwise remain hidden from politicians.

content.headline: Rail faults to cause Danish delays and cancellations from Monday
content.shortHeadline: Danish rail delays and cancellations begin Monday amid track faults
content.standfirst: Banedanmark says an unusually high number of rail faults will require speed limits and cancelled regional services from Monday. Changes are expected to last until 29 November while the infrastructure is assessed.

image.caption: Track faults and damage to signalling equipment will disrupt Danish train services.

sources.originalTitle: Ekstraordinært antal skinnefejl fører til forsinkelser og færre tog mellem København og Fredericia

segments.body: Banedanmark plans speed restrictions on several routes from Monday after finding 50% more rail faults than in a normal year. Regional trains between Odense and Fredericia will be cancelled and replaced with buses; some other services will also be affected. The agency expects a journey from Copenhagen to Fredericia could take about 15 minutes longer.

segments.title: What passengers should know
segments.body: The restrictions are expected to remain until 29 November, when Banedanmark will assess whether normal service can resume. The agency also cites a fire-damaged technical hut near Aarup, which has already affected signalling on Funen. It says the speed limits reduce the risk of rail breaks and advises passengers to check Rejseplanen before travelling.

content.headline: Pochettino confirmed as Manchester United manager after emotional USA exit
content.shortHeadline: Pochettino confirmed at Man Utd after tearful USA farewell
content.standfirst: Mauricio Pochettino will take charge at Old Trafford on 18 November, replacing Michael Carrick. He says leaving the USA job was one of the most difficult decisions of his career.

image.caption: Mauricio Pochettino became emotional during a USA news conference.

sources.originalTitle: Tearful Pochettino on 'difficult' decision to leave USA for Man Utd
Fitness obsessed & 'control freak' - what can Man Utd expect from Pochettino?

segments.body: Manchester United have confirmed Pochettino as their new manager, with the Argentine set to begin on 18 November and contracted until June 2029. He became emotional at a news conference as he described leaving the USA national team as a very sad decision, but said the chance to manage United was difficult to turn down.

segments.title: A demanding approach
segments.body: Toby Alderweireld, who played under Pochettino at Tottenham, says the manager puts the team first and expects players to follow his plan. He also points to a gruelling fitness regime and a high-intensity, front-foot style.

perspectives.body: Alderweireld describes Pochettino as a positive “control freak”, saying he closely follows players’ work on and off the pitch.

content.headline: France edge South Africa 21-19 in Nations Championship thriller
content.shortHeadline: France hold off South Africa in 21-19 thriller
content.standfirst: France ended a five-match losing run against the world champions in Paris, holding on after South Africa fought back in a chaotic second half. The result also strengthens France’s position in the northern hemisphere standings.

sources.originalTitle: France hold nerve to edge past South Africa in thriller

segments.body: France beat South Africa 21-19 at Stade de France, ending their five-match losing run against the world champions. Antoine Dupont’s side scored three tries in an electric first half, with Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang, Theo Attissogbe and Louis Bielle-Biarrey crossing.

segments.title: A tense finish
segments.body: South Africa rallied after Jasper Wiese was shown a 20-minute red card, with replacement Cobus Reinach and Malcolm Marx scoring tries. Manie Libbok missed the conversion that would have levelled the match, and France held on under late pressure.

The victory dents South Africa’s hopes of reaching the Nations Championship final and leaves France six points clear at the top of the northern hemisphere standings. Les Bleus face Argentina next Saturday.

content.headline: McGinn double gives Scotland 2-1 win over North Macedonia
content.shortHeadline: McGinn scores twice as Scotland beat North Macedonia
content.standfirst: Scotland earned a first home win under Sebastien Pocognoli, but a narrow victory over the group’s bottom side did little to quiet doubts about the team’s progress. Andy Robertson also drew level with Kenny Dalglish’s cap record.

sources.originalTitle: Tough watch as Scotland again battle against their own limitations
Scotland Men's Football Team

segments.body: John McGinn scored twice as Scotland beat North Macedonia 2-1 at Hampden, giving manager Sebastien Pocognoli his first home win. The hosts led after McGinn’s second-half opener, but Elmin Rastoder equalised before McGinn converted a late penalty won by Ben Gannon-Doak.

segments.title: A win with work still to do
segments.body: The result leaves Scotland one point behind Slovenia with one group game remaining. Scotland must travel to Switzerland, while Slovenia visit North Macedonia. Robertson won his 102nd cap, drawing level with Dalglish’s Scotland record.

perspectives.body: BBC Sport’s match analysis described the performance as a difficult watch, arguing that Scotland’s effort outweighed its precision and that the team still looks uncertain in its system.

content.headline: Svitolina ends Sabalenka's season to reach WTA Finals semi-finals
content.shortHeadline: Svitolina beats Sabalenka to reach WTA Finals last four
content.standfirst: Elina Svitolina recovered from losing the second set to defeat Aryna Sabalenka in three, ending the former world number one’s campaign at the season-ending event. Svitolina advances to face Linda Noskova.

image.caption: Aryna Sabalenka reacts during her WTA Finals campaign.

sources.originalTitle: Sabalenka's season ended by Svitolina at WTA Finals

segments.body: Elina Svitolina beat Aryna Sabalenka 6-3 3-6 6-1 to reach the WTA Finals semi-finals and end Sabalenka’s season. The Ukrainian recovered her composure in the deciding set, winning the final six games as Sabalenka’s frustration grew.

Svitolina, who is playing the tournament for the first time since reaching the 2019 final, will meet Linda Noskova in the last four. Mirra Andreeva, who finished top of the group, faces Jessica Pegula in the other semi-final.

content.headline: Beardman takes record 6-24 on debut as Australia thrash England
content.shortHeadline: Beardman takes record ODI debut figures against England
content.standfirst: Mahli Beardman took 6-24 in his first one-day international, the best figures by an Australian on debut in the format, as Australia crushed England in Perth. The 21-year-old’s performance also brought fresh attention to Australia’s next generation of fast bowlers.

image.caption: Mahli Beardman, player of the match in the 2024 Under-19 World Cup final.

sources.originalTitle: Surfing speedster Beardman gives a glimpse of Ashes future

segments.body: Mahli Beardman took 6-24 on his one-day international debut as Australia thrashed England in Perth. It is the best bowling return by an Australian on an ODI debut. The 21-year-old dismissed Harry Brook, Joe Root and Jordan Cox among his six victims.

segments.title: A glimpse of what may follow
segments.body: Beardman bowled at an average of 86.5mph and reached 90.6mph, his fastest delivery recorded. His progress has been carefully managed after two back stress injuries, and the report notes his immediate future is expected to be in white-ball cricket.

content.headline: England beat France to win third Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup
content.shortHeadline: England beat France to win a third wheelchair world title
content.standfirst: England came back from a 22-10 deficit to beat France 50-38 in Wollongong, becoming the first nation to win the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup three times and retaining the trophy they claimed in 2022.

image.caption: England celebrate becoming Wheelchair Rugby League world champions for the third time.

sources.originalTitle: Sharks, ladders and a four-year plan - how England won World Cup

segments.body: England beat France 50-38 in the final in Wollongong to win the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup for a third time. Tom Coyd’s side had trailed 22-10 before tries from Rob Hawkins and Jack Brown helped turn the match around.

segments.title: An attacking mindset
segments.body: Coyd said England had avoided framing the campaign as a defence of their 2022 title, instead encouraging an attacking approach. The team scored 386 points across the group stage and semi-finals while conceding 68, before becoming the first nation to win the wheelchair tournament three times.

content.headline: Owono receives 12-match ban after fatal collision with De Miguel
content.shortHeadline: Owono handed 12-match ban after De Miguel’s death
content.standfirst: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono has been suspended for 12 matches by the Spanish football federation after his collision with Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel, who died the following day. The federation has also ruled that the abandoned match will not be replayed.

image.caption: Jesus Owono plays for Equatorial Guinea.

sources.originalTitle: Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision gets 12-game ban

segments.body: Jesus Owono has received a 12-match suspension from the Spanish football federation’s disciplinary committee after the collision with Jesus de Miguel during a second-tier match on 2 November. De Miguel, 30, died the next day.

segments.title: The match will stand
segments.body: The federation said it based its disciplinary decision on the referee’s report, which recorded that Owono was sent off for striking an opponent in the chest with excessive force. Separately, it ruled the abandoned match would not be replayed; the 2-2 score will stand.

content.headline: Hendon prepare to return after death of team-mate Ezekiel Williams
content.shortHeadline: Hendon prepare to play again after Williams’s death
content.standfirst: The non-league club will return to action for the first time since midfielder Ezekiel Williams died aged 26. Players and staff are mourning a team-mate who had joined only weeks earlier and was also a football coach.

image.caption: Ezekiel Williams, described by Hendon’s chairman as a high-energy midfielder.

sources.originalTitle: The club preparing to play again after the death of a player

segments.body: Hendon are preparing to play for the first time since midfielder Ezekiel Williams died in hospital on 2 November from head injuries after an incident in Milton Keynes. Williams, 26, joined the club in September and had scored in a league match shortly before his death.

segments.title: A club grieving together
segments.body: Players and staff have been offered counselling as they prepare to return. Hendon chairman Cyrus Cooper says the club is struggling to come to terms with what happened, while midfielder Tashae Andall-Gibbons says the team-mate’s absence will be felt on match day. Two men have been charged with murder.

content.headline: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul turn grief into a more personal pop record
content.shortHeadline: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul make a more personal record
content.standfirst: The Belgian art-pop duo’s next album follows the loss of both their fathers and Pupul’s mother. Their sharp humour remains, but the songs also make room for grief, family life and a sound they began shaping in Martinique.

image.caption: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Would you breastfeed your own father?’ The goofy, spiky world of art-pop duo Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul

segments.body: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul’s second album, Mainland Madinina, moves from the political wit of their debut towards more intimate subjects. Both musicians have lost parents since making Topical Dancer: Pupul’s mother died, and Adigéry’s father, who had Alzheimer’s, also died.

segments.title: A different kind of openness
segments.body: The pair began writing in Martinique, where Adigéry’s parents moved from, making stripped-back demos with an acoustic guitar. The record keeps their comic edge, but also follows them through grief, growing older and raising children. Adigéry says one song records her finally throwing away flowers from her father’s funeral.

Soulwax, whose Deewee studio helped shape the duo’s earlier work, again co-produced the album. Pupul says its members helped the pair test the intentions behind their writing. The new record is due in February.

content.headline: Sheherazaad’s debut transforms Urdu folk into eerie, reverb-heavy music
content.shortHeadline: Sheherazaad turns Urdu folk into eerie, reverb-heavy music
content.standfirst: The South Asian-American singer and composer builds a dark, introspective sound from Urdu vocals and sparse acoustic arrangements. The review praises her virtuosic singing, while finding some spoken-word passages overly theatrical.

image.caption: Sheherazaad.

sources.originalTitle: Sheherazaad: Khudgarzi review – Urdu folk acoustics transformed by an eerie haze of grunge

segments.body: On Khudgarzi, Sheherazaad draws on classical singing traditions from her heritage, shaping them into a disquieting debut. Reverb hangs over sparse arrangements: tabla echoes beneath her keening voice on “Qatil”, while “Registaan” turns a simple guitar figure unnerving.

segments.title: Voice in the haze
segments.body: The review hears shades of PJ Harvey’s eerie grunge and Massive Attack’s work with Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan in the album’s atmosphere. Sheherazaad’s voice is the anchor, shifting from a husky lower register to full-throated melisma and electronic processing.

The reviewer finds the whispered spoken-word sections less successful, but describes the blend of tabla, folk strings, cello, guitar and other instruments as engrossing. The result is a debut that turns away from bright, explosive dynamics in favour of a sombre, inward sound.

content.headline: Blackhaine’s debut is a punishing plunge into noise and UK rap
content.shortHeadline: Blackhaine’s debut swallows the listener in noise and UK rap
content.standfirst: Tom Heyes’s first album as Blackhaine stretches between UK rap and extreme electronics, building an oppressive sound around working-class despondency. The review finds its intensity unsettling, but also hard to imitate.

image.caption: Blackhaine.

sources.originalTitle: Blackhaine: Saints in the Wethouse review – spectacularly intense UK rap that will swallow you up and wring you out

segments.body: Saints in the Wethouse is an uncompromising debut from Tom Heyes, the Salford artist known as Blackhaine. His music joins UK drill to extreme electronics, with distorted bass, feedback and garbled vocals that sound less like conventional boasts than a voice under pressure.

segments.title: A sound that overwhelms
segments.body: The album’s harshest passages abandon rhythm for walls of noise and screams. Even a melodic acoustic song, “The Wind”, feels unsettling in its surroundings. The review links the record’s sound to lyrics about mental illness, substance use, rage and despondency.

Heyes has worked with Playboi Carti and presented work at major art institutions, but the reviewer argues that his music remains far from the mainstream. Its force, the review suggests, lies in a sound so intense that it seems to overwhelm everything around it.

content.headline: Manfred Honeck makes a forceful first statement with the Philharmonia
content.shortHeadline: Manfred Honeck makes a forceful first statement with the Philharmonia
content.standfirst: The orchestra’s principal conductor designate, who takes up the post in 2028, led a programme spanning Johann Strauss II, Mozart and Richard Strauss. The review hears a confident preview of the partnership to come.

image.caption: Manfred Honeck with the Philharmonia Orchestra.

sources.originalTitle: Philharmonia/Honeck/Ax review – principal conductor designate gives a scorching taste of things to come

segments.body: Manfred Honeck’s Philharmonia concert opened with a Fledermaus Overture whose elegance and mischievous pace set an assured tone. The Austrian conductor, a former violist, led from memory and drew an evidently responsive performance from the orchestra.

segments.title: From Mozart to Elektra
segments.body: Emanuel Ax was the lucid soloist in Mozart’s Piano Concerto No 25, balancing sweetness with seriousness. Honeck then turned to his own suite from Richard Strauss’s Elektra, bringing out its turbulent strings and a finale the reviewer describes as deliciously bloody.

Honeck becomes the Philharmonia’s principal conductor in 2028, only the seventh to hold the role in the orchestra’s 81-year history. The reviewer calls the programme a clear statement of intent and a compelling taste of what the appointment may bring.

content.headline: Rita Wilson’s new album finds a voice beyond Hollywood’s roles for women
content.shortHeadline: Rita Wilson finds a voice beyond Hollywood’s roles for women
content.standfirst: The actor and producer says typecasting as a mother or wife left her creatively dissatisfied, helping prompt a later turn to songwriting. Her new album explores women’s lives, ageing, illness and the possibility of becoming someone new.

image.caption: Rita Wilson.

sources.originalTitle: Rita Wilson: ‘My body turned on me – but it was also there to heal me’

segments.body: Rita Wilson says her sixth album, Sound of a Woman, follows a woman’s life through love, loss, ageing and self-acceptance. She began pursuing music in her fifties, after finding that many of the acting roles offered to her had become repetitive and centred on supportive wives, mothers and friends.

segments.title: A different way to speak
segments.body: Wilson says songwriting gave her a way to express things that her acting roles had not asked her to say. She describes the film and television business as ageist and says she would once have been afraid to speak publicly about that. Her songs also address her experience of breast cancer and a bilateral mastectomy.

The album includes “Your Mother”, inspired by Wilson’s relationship with her late mother, and “Spare Keys”, which she describes as a break-up with her old self. She says she is also expected to return to her role in a planned Girls reboot, though the details remain unconfirmed in the interview.

content.headline: Taylor Swift’s earliest fans remember finding her on MySpace
content.shortHeadline: Taylor Swift’s earliest fans remember finding her on MySpace
content.standfirst: Twenty years after Swift’s debut, a former teenage fan recalls the online community that grew around a young country singer before she became a global star. The essay explores how her direct connection with fans helped make them feel part of her rise.

image.caption: Taylor Swift as a teenage country singer.

sources.originalTitle: The Taylor Swift I knew on MySpace in 2006

segments.body: Before Taylor Swift was a global star, a teenage fan found her through a MySpace recommendation and began following her songs and updates. The writer recalls trading comments, collecting press clippings and sharing the excitement of a young singer who seemed close to her audience.

segments.title: A fan community grows
segments.body: Swift’s self-titled debut, released in 2006, offered songs about teenage romance and uncertainty. The essay recalls how fans used lyrics on their profiles and treated her early interviews and blog posts as a window into a life they felt they could relate to.

The writer recognises that Swift had a skilled promotional team and protective parents around her. But the early relationship felt personal to fans, who could watch her career gather momentum and imagine that their own ambitions might also be possible.

content.headline: Armand Hammer’s Snakes & Ladders turns everyday scenes into political art
content.shortHeadline: Armand Hammer turn everyday scenes into political art
content.standfirst: The New York rap duo’s surprise album pairs billy woods and Elucid’s dense writing with production from collaborators in the indie-rap scene they helped nurture. Pitchfork hears a work that binds present-day anxiety to a longer history of Black political art.

sources.originalTitle: Snakes & Ladders

segments.body: On Snakes & Ladders, billy woods and Elucid turn fragments of ordinary life into sharp, layered writing. A walk down a street or a job application becomes a way to describe the pressures of power, race and technology.

segments.title: A collective sound
segments.body: The album brings in a wide group of producers, including clipping., Preservation and Kenny Segal. Their varied beats move between spare piano, jagged percussion and jazz-inflected sounds, but the review finds a shared atmosphere across the record.

Pitchfork situates the duo’s work within a tradition of Black political art, connecting their present-day writing to earlier writers and artists. The review argues that the album responds to anxieties about rap’s future by emphasising culture and language rather than commercial measures.

content.headline: Grumpy’s Unfindable Ring makes room for love, gender and musical play
content.shortHeadline: Grumpy mix Americana and gender trouble on Unfindable Ring
content.standfirst: The Brooklyn group moves between country, folk, electronica and art pop while writing from the perspective of a trans couple. Pitchfork finds a record whose playfulness and romantic devotion coexist with the hostility its characters face.

sources.originalTitle: Unfindable Ring

segments.body: Grumpy’s Unfindable Ring opens with a song about a trans couple whose happiness is challenged by a stranger at a gas station. The encounter darkens its chorus, but the review finds that it also makes the couple’s love feel more resolute.

segments.title: An unruly Americana
segments.body: The Brooklyn six-piece draws on country, folk, electronica, indie rock and art pop. Frontman Heaven Schmitt shifts between a twang and Auto-Tune, while the arrangements fracture familiar genre cues rather than settling into one sound.

With the exception of the drummer, the band members are trans. The review argues that this perspective shapes the album’s world without reducing it to a single theme: songs move from gendered hostility to tender love, including “Twenty Five”, an imagined message of support to a partner’s younger self.

content.headline: Robert Pattinson is reportedly a leading Bond contender as Amazon weighs its 007
content.shortHeadline: Pattinson reportedly leads the race to become the next James Bond
content.standfirst: Industry reporting says Amazon MGM may favour the actor, who is said to have been offered a shorter commitment and a larger fee than other contenders. No casting decision has been announced; a companion look at Bond reveals how past unveilings have gone awry.

image.caption: Robert Pattinson, one of the reported contenders for James Bond.

sources.originalTitle: Robert Pattinson reportedly leads James Bond contenders
‘It was a train wreck! I was terrified’: how the new James Bond will be announced – and what can go wrong

segments.body: Robert Pattinson has emerged as a possible favourite to play James Bond, according to reporting by Puck’s Matthew Belloni. The report says his proposed deal would cover three films, rather than the four reportedly offered to other actors, and include a larger, unspecified fee.

segments.title: A high-profile handover
segments.body: Pattinson is among five reported contenders, alongside Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Nicholas Hoult. Amazon MGM has not announced its choice. Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next Bond film, with Steven Knight writing the script.

segments.title: The announcement is part of the spectacle
segments.body: The Guardian’s account of previous Bond reveals recalls the awkward launch of Daniel Craig in 2005, when a lifejacket during a speedboat arrival became a media talking point. A publicist quoted in the report says the event was assembled at short notice after a leak.

perspectives.body: The casting story is also a story about publicity: Amazon MGM could choose a traditional press event or reveal its new Bond through social media, where a casting announcement would quickly become a global spectacle.

content.headline: Darth Vader’s Star Wars lightsaber sells at auction for nearly $5m
content.shortHeadline: Darth Vader’s lightsaber sells for nearly $5m
content.standfirst: The screen-used prop from The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi set a reported auction record for a Star Wars item. It was used in the series’ famous “I am your father” scene and sold for far more than the estimate.

image.caption: Darth Vader’s lightsaber used in The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi.

sources.originalTitle: Darth Vader’s lightsaber, used in Star Wars movies The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi, sells for nearly $5m

segments.body: A lightsaber used by Darth Vader in The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi sold for $4.875m at a US auction on Thursday. The prop appeared in the famous “I am your father” scene in the 1980 film.

Heritage Auctions said the sale set a record for a screen-used Star Wars prop. The item had been estimated to sell for more than $1m, and surpassed the previous reported record: Luke Skywalker’s lightsaber and severed hand, sold for $3.75m in July.

content.headline: To Hold a Mountain follows a Montenegrin herder’s fight to protect her home
content.shortHeadline: A Montenegrin herder fights to protect her mountain home
content.standfirst: Mileva “Gara” Jovanović became a prominent opponent of plans for a NATO training area on her summer pastures. The award-winning documentary follows her work, her family and a way of life whose future remains uncertain even after the military plan was cancelled.

image.caption: Mileva “Gara” Jovanović with her daughter, Nada, in To Hold a Mountain.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Goats are good. They listen’: the herder who defeated Montenegro’s military – and can identify her cows’ herby burps

segments.body: To Hold a Mountain follows Gara Jovanović, a herder in Montenegro’s Sinjajevina mountains. She became a public voice against a plan to turn part of the pastureland into a NATO training and weapons-testing area, and the filmmakers spent years documenting her demanding seasonal work.

segments.title: A life built around the mountain
segments.body: The film observes Jovanović caring for animals, moving between high pastures and winter homes, and raising her daughter Nada. Jovanović says the mountain offers freedom she did not find in city work. She sees it not only as a livelihood, but as a living presence she feels bound to defend.

The filmmakers reopened the edit after the government cancelled its military plans in 2025, turning the film from a campaign against a possible takeover into a record of victory. The documentary also considers the economic pressures on pastoral life and whether younger generations can sustain it.

content.headline: Wicker’s strange romance asks what a perfect husband is for
content.shortHeadline: Wicker’s strange romance turns the perfect husband into a provocation
content.standfirst: Olivia Colman’s Fisherwoman pays for a husband made of willow, and the film turns the absurd premise into a bawdy fairy tale about desire and domestic labour. The review enjoys its excess while questioning the husband’s lack of agency.

image.caption: Olivia Colman’s Fisherwoman with the husband made of wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it

segments.body: In Wicker, an ostracised fisherwoman played by Olivia Colman commissions a basketmaker to make her a husband. Alexander Skarsgård’s willow-built creation is attentive, attractive and willing to help, prompting envy and suspicion in the village around them.

segments.title: A fantasy with a catch
segments.body: The review calls the film a knowingly sexist, gleefully horny comedy: its husband is expected to meet his wife’s every need, even when he says he is flammable or faces danger. That premise raises a question the film only partly addresses—whether devotion can be love when the devoted partner has so little freedom.

The reviewer nevertheless finds a comic charge in the reversal of familiar expectations of women’s servitude. Colman’s character is described as relieved, rather than entitled, to have a partner who is kind and does not expect her to be subordinate. The film works best, the review suggests, as a fairy tale and a provocation rather than a lecture.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning turns Facebook’s failures into a horror story
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning makes Facebook’s failures feel like horror
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to The Social Network dramatises reporting on Facebook’s internal files and their effects on users and politics. The review’s personal unease comes from recognising the gap between the revelations and its own continued use of Meta’s platforms.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling

segments.body: The Social Reckoning centres on Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz and former Facebook employee Frances Haugen, whose disclosures helped expose company research and practices around content, teenage users’ mental health and political misinformation.

segments.title: The fear comes home
segments.body: The review describes Sorkin’s film as an investigative journalism story with the tension of a horror film. Its account follows Facebook’s recommendation systems and the company’s responses to concerns, while placing Mark Zuckerberg’s insistence that the platform is not responsible for what users post at the centre of the argument.

The writer’s strongest response is not simply fear but discomfort at how easily the film’s revelations coexist with everyday use of Meta products. The story, the review argues, exposes a cycle in which outrage and attention are monetised even as many users feel unable to leave.

content.headline: Oasis reunion film captures the euphoria but leaves the family story out
content.shortHeadline: Oasis reunion film captures the euphoria, not the reconciliation
content.standfirst: Steven Knight’s documentary follows the Gallaghers’ 2025 tour and the fans who travelled to see it. The review praises its concert footage but says the film avoids the questions of how the brothers made peace and what brought them back together.

image.caption: Oasis in Steven Knight’s reunion documentary.

sources.originalTitle: Oasis fans’ most important question remains unanswered

segments.body: Don’t Look Back in Anger follows Oasis around the world during their 2025 reunion tour. The review finds the concert footage and the fans’ response moving, showing the band’s songs connecting with listeners across generations and continents.

segments.title: The missing part of the reunion
segments.body: The film moves from a short account of the band’s history to rehearsals, leaving much of the preceding 15 years unexplained. The reviewer says it does not show the conversations or reconciliation that led the Gallagher brothers to tour together again, and gives little attention to the ticket-pricing controversy.

The documentary does show the brothers speaking warmly about each other and their changed relationship. But the reviewer argues that its theme of forgiveness is less persuasive without a fuller account of what had to be forgiven.

content.headline: Ebenezer gives Johnny Depp a Scrooge role and a comeback narrative
content.shortHeadline: Ebenezer casts Johnny Depp as Scrooge—and as a comeback story
content.standfirst: Ti West’s new Dickens adaptation gives Depp a major studio lead after years away from studio films. The Guardian review finds him more convincing as the unreformed miser, while BBC reporting examines the controversy and calculated comeback campaign around his casting.

image.caption: Johnny Depp as Scrooge in Ebenezer.

sources.originalTitle: Ebenezer review – Johnny Depp’s Scrooge tries to exorcise ghosts of business past
'Cancelled' star Johnny Depp is making a big Hollywood comeback - will it succeed?

segments.body: Johnny Depp plays Scrooge in Ebenezer, a new adaptation of A Christmas Carol directed by Ti West. The Guardian review finds the film a faithful, watchable version of Dickens, with a new prologue featuring Ian McKellen as Marley and some changes to the story’s supporting characters.

segments.title: The film and the public image
segments.body: The review finds Depp effective as the bad-tempered, unredeemed Scrooge, but less affecting once the character changes. The BBC’s wider account notes that the film’s publicity has framed his return to a major studio as a comeback, a framing that has drawn criticism as well as enthusiastic responses from some viewers.

perspectives.body: The BBC examines how Depp’s casting carries a post-trial public-image debate. It reports contrasting views: one critic calls the comeback campaign tasteless, while a publicist argues that commercial prospects and audience response will determine whether the return succeeds.

segments.body: The BBC reports that the film’s Scrooge make-up may help separate the character from the actor’s public image, and that industry forecasts anticipated a potentially solid box office. Those projections and audience expectations are not the same as a confirmed outcome.

content.headline: Renate Reinsve recalls the role that nearly came after she quit acting
content.shortHeadline: Renate Reinsve on the role that changed her life
content.standfirst: The Norwegian actor thought The Worst Person in the World would be her final film before director Joachim Trier offered her the lead. She reflects on the recognition it brought, the collaborative shoot and the challenge of playing a very different woman in Fjord.

image.caption: Renate Reinsve.

sources.originalTitle: 'It stopped me quitting acting': Renate Reinsve on her life-changing role in The Worst Person in the World

segments.body: Renate Reinsve had been considering leaving acting when Joachim Trier called with the lead role in The Worst Person in the World. The film became a breakthrough, winning her the Cannes best actress award and bringing international attention to her performance as the unsettled Julie.

segments.title: A character people recognised
segments.body: Reinsve says she recognised parts of herself in Julie, who changes careers and relationships while approaching 30. She recalls a playful shoot in Oslo and says the film’s honesty helped people feel less alone in recognising complicated, sometimes unflattering emotions.

In Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord, Reinsve plays Lisbet, an evangelical Christian whose children are removed amid allegations of abuse. She describes the character as quiet and unlike herself, and says the film asks audiences to question their assumptions rather than telling them what to think.

content.headline: Ade Adepitan joins I’m a Celebrity as its first wheelchair-using contestant
content.shortHeadline: Ade Adepitan becomes I’m a Celebrity’s first wheelchair user
content.standfirst: The Paralympian and presenter says he helped producers assess access at the camp before taking part. He hopes the programme will prompt discussion about disability, while facing ableist criticism of the adaptations made for him.

image.caption: Ade Adepitan, who is joining I’m a Celebrity.

sources.originalTitle: ‘You can’t train to be chucked in a box full of rats!’ Ade Adepitan on fear, facing down sharks and being I’m a Celeb’s first wheelchair user

segments.body: Ade Adepitan is set to become the first wheelchair user on I’m a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here!. The Paralympic medallist and television presenter visited the camp to advise producers on access, including different terrain, narrow paths and the need to transfer from his chair in some areas.

segments.title: A public conversation
segments.body: Adepitan says he is aware some people may frame his access arrangements as an advantage, but compares the challenge to the problem-solving disabled people face in everyday life. He says taking part is not about representing every disabled person, but could make disability more visible to viewers.

Adepitan has also described barriers he has encountered in London, including broken station lifts and taxi drivers refusing to take his wheelchair. He says those experiences are created by physical and social barriers, not by his wheelchair itself.

content.headline: The Body turns Catholic schoolgirl drama into camp supernatural television
content.shortHeadline: The Body makes Catholic schoolgirl drama camp and uncanny
content.standfirst: Set in 2004, the series mixes teen rivalry, sexual tension and an occult party gone wrong. The review praises its energetic, queer-centred take on familiar high-school tropes, though it finds the eight episodes overlong.

image.caption: The cast of The Body.

sources.originalTitle: The Body review – this sexy retro high school drama is like Cruel Intentions … with added Satanic rituals

segments.body: Netflix’s The Body begins at a Catholic school in 2004, where a Halloween party at an abandoned convent ends with a girl comatose and other students suffering hallucinations and seizures. The event upends the school’s social order and pulls its outcasts and popular girls into a shared mystery.

segments.title: Teenage drama under the supernatural
segments.body: The review sees echoes of Cruel Intentions and other early-2000s teen films, but says creator Quinn Shephard gives familiar types more complicated edges. The show connects adolescent social rules with religious codes, and follows the girls’ sexuality, rivalry and shifting loyalties alongside the possibility of something supernatural.

The series’ period details include instant messaging, low-rise fashion and music by Kelly Clarkson, Ciara and Sean Paul. The reviewer finds its camp mood and big emotions enjoyable, while arguing that the pacing could be tighter and some male characters less peripheral.

content.headline: 12 12 12 turns an implausible heist into an entertaining chase
content.shortHeadline: 12 12 12 is an implausible but entertaining heist thriller
content.standfirst: Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan lead a Swiss-bank robbery story told across three timelines. The review relishes its contortionist opening and elaborate set pieces, while finding its central 12-day premise hard to believe.

image.caption: Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan in 12 12 12.

sources.originalTitle: 12 12 12 review – Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s super fun heist hunt

segments.body: 12 12 12 follows a robbery planned over 12 months, carried out in 12 hours and pursued for 12 days. Jamie Dornan plays a criminal pulled back into the job, while Anthony Mackie is the FBI agent tracking him across Europe.

segments.title: Three clocks, one chase
segments.body: Each episode moves between the planning, the robbery and the investigation. The review praises the series’ slick structure and set pieces, from a contortionist emerging from a bank vault to the crew’s use of a drill, a diverted train and jet-skis.

The show’s central rule—that robbers not caught within 12 days tend not to be caught at all—strains credibility, as does the speed with which the FBI agent finds clues. The reviewer recommends suspending disbelief, but says the series’ other familiar crime-drama elements offer little surprise.

content.headline: Cunk on Cinema makes film history gloriously, deliberately wrong
content.shortHeadline: Cunk on Cinema is a hilariously wrong guide to film history
content.standfirst: Diane Morgan’s deadpan interviewer returns with a three-part mockumentary that baffles film-makers and critics with confidently absurd questions. The review enjoys its relentless silliness while noting that the series offers only a sketch of cinema history.

image.caption: Diane Morgan as Philomena Cunk.

sources.originalTitle: Cunk on Cinema review – Diane Morgan baffles Hollywood with some of the stupidest jokes ever told

segments.body: Cunk on Cinema sends Diane Morgan’s Philomena Cunk through a three-part history of film, asking experts questions that confuse basic facts and names. Its opening list of human achievements includes “growing the great wall of Chinese” and “discovering Mona Lisa”.

segments.title: Prank, with a purpose
segments.body: The review sees the series as a prank show whose pleasure comes partly from watching interviewees respond. British participants may know Cunk’s routine, but American guests Michael Bay and Steven E. de Souza appear more straightforwardly baffled by her tangents.

The series offers a loose tour through movements including German expressionism and the French New Wave, but the review is clear that viewers should not expect a serious film-history lesson. Its strongest achievement is a steady run of absurd jokes, including Cunk’s detours into AI and her mangling of famous names.

content.headline: What to stream this week: from The Altruists to Yellowjackets
content.shortHeadline: What to stream: The Altruists, Yellowjackets and more
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s weekly guide ranges from a Sam Bankman-Fried drama to the final season of Yellowjackets. It also picks a documentary about overdose-prevention volunteers and a new series about a Christian drama of Jesus.

image.caption: Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison and Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

sources.originalTitle: The Altruists to Yellowjackets: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The Altruists dramatises the rise and fall of FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried and his colleague Caroline Ellison. The guide calls its story of tech idealism and risk-taking relevant, though it finds the series somewhat staid and dated.

segments.title: Final seasons and other lives
segments.body: Yellowjackets returns for its fourth and final season, with the guide questioning whether the show can bring its past and present timelines together. Other picks include Rewarding, a Belfast comedy-drama about under-resourced care workers, and the penultimate run of the faith-centred series The Chosen.

The selection also includes The Hotline, a documentary about volunteers who stay on the phone with people using drugs and contact emergency services when needed. The guide highlights its emphasis on trust and empathy in overdose prevention.

content.headline: I’m a Celebrity’s new line-up opts for familiar faces over controversy
content.shortHeadline: I’m a Celebrity’s line-up swaps controversy for familiar faces
content.standfirst: The i argues that this year’s contestants are a welcome change from politicians who used the jungle to rehabilitate their images. Its case is that likeable campmates can make entertaining television without manufactured controversy.

image.caption: Ant and Dec return to host I’m a Celebrity.

sources.originalTitle: I’m a Celeb has finally learned its lesson

segments.body: This year’s I’m a Celebrity line-up includes Wayne Rooney, Kaiser Chiefs singer Ricky Wilson, presenter Joanna Page, AJ Odudu and Paralympian Ade Adepitan. The i’s columnist welcomes a group she sees as less controversial than some recent contestants.

segments.title: The case against political contestants
segments.body: The piece criticises the show’s earlier choices of politicians Nigel Farage and Matt Hancock, arguing that their appearances helped them present themselves to viewers as ordinary and approachable. It suggests reality television can play a role in shaping political reputations.

The columnist acknowledges the concern that a less divisive cast could mean less drama, but points to the previous series as evidence that campmates getting along can be enjoyable to watch. Whether this year’s group avoids controversy remains to be seen.

content.headline: Patricia Hodge on Miranda, playing Thatcher and becoming a mother later
content.shortHeadline: Patricia Hodge on Miranda, Thatcher and becoming a mother
content.standfirst: The actor reflects on roles from The Life and Loves of a She-Devil to Miranda, and on the long struggle to have children. At 79, she also discusses how her view of her career has changed with family life.

image.caption: Patricia Hodge.

sources.originalTitle: Patricia Hodge on conceiving at 45: ‘It was a test of endurance’

segments.body: Patricia Hodge is often cast as a cool, aristocratic figure, but the interview finds a warm comic presence behind roles including Miranda’s Penny. She recalls a career that has moved between stage, television and characters such as Margaret Thatcher.

segments.title: Playing women in public life
segments.body: For her portrayal of Thatcher, Hodge says she avoided imitation and thought instead about a woman trying to be taken seriously among men. She also credits Miranda with helping women feel more comfortable laughing at themselves.
Hodge says she struggled to conceive before having her first child at 42 and her second at 45. She is now a grandmother of two; the interview took place on the day her second grandson was born.

content.headline: Gentle Monster to Conclave: seven films to watch on television
content.shortHeadline: Seven films to watch on television this week
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s guide selects a family drama, a Nashville mystery and a string of older films available to stream or watch on television. Its picks range from Léa Seydoux in Gentle Monster to Ralph Fiennes in Conclave.

image.caption: Léa Seydoux in Gentle Monster.

sources.originalTitle: Gentle Monster to Conclave: the seven best films to watch on TV this week

segments.body: The guide leads with Gentle Monster, a family drama in which Léa Seydoux’s character’s life changes after police arrest her partner. The selection also recommends Jessica Chastain’s country-music mystery Heartland, currently available on Netflix.

segments.title: From classics to recent dramas
segments.body: Other choices include Akira Kurosawa’s Ran, a retelling of King Lear set amid Japan’s feudal wars, and Edward Berger’s Conclave, a thriller about the secretive process of choosing a pope. The guide also picks Eileen, a story of female desire and liberation, and a documentary about men wrongly convicted of murder.

The week’s final selection is The Dead Don’t Hurt, a western directed by and starring Viggo Mortensen. The recommendations span different eras and styles, with broadcast and streaming details attached to each title in the original guide.

content.headline: Artists make satirical games to push back against Trump’s political propaganda
content.shortHeadline: Artists turn political propaganda into satirical games
content.standfirst: As the White House uses browser games to promote its agenda, developers and activists are making playable responses. Their projects borrow familiar arcade forms to mock policy, political messaging and the gamification of public life.

image.caption: A scene from The Secret Handshake’s Operation Epic Furious.

sources.originalTitle: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda

segments.body: The Trump White House’s online Arcade has recast familiar games such as Tetris and Snake as political messaging. In response, artists and developers have made satirical games that turn the same formats back on the administration.

segments.title: A different kind of play
segments.body: The Secret Handshake collective’s Operation Epic Furious: Strait to Hell asks players to choose between ordering Diet Coke and invading Iran, then follows the president through an unwinnable adventure. The group says it made the game because the administration had already used games to make war seem entertaining.

Other projects, including Tax Evaders and Corrupt Invaders, use arcade-style play to comment on public spending, corruption and the cost of living. Their makers say familiar mechanics can make political headlines feel different, while acknowledging that satire and the administration’s own propaganda use the same medium.

content.headline: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer finds quiet magic in fixing a small town
content.shortHeadline: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer makes restoration a gentle pleasure
content.standfirst: A raccoon dog on a BMX repairs a shrine and delivers parcels in a small Japanese town. The review finds the game’s daily routines calming and absorbing, despite some clumsy mini-games.

image.caption: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer.

sources.originalTitle: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – an adorable raccoon mends the world, one parcel at a time

segments.body: In Tanuki: Pon’s Summer, the player takes a post-office job to help pay for restoring an old shrine before a local festival. Most days involve collecting parcels and cycling through a rural town to deliver them, with small repairs and errands gradually drawing the community together.

segments.title: The pleasure of a familiar route
segments.body: The review finds satisfaction in learning the paths and routines of the town, eventually knowing the way without relying on the map. The BMX is a particular pleasure, opening up chances to explore and find routes through the landscape.

Some mini-games, including fishing and chopping logs, can feel awkward to control. But the review argues that the game’s gentle pace and focus on repair make it rewarding to linger in its world rather than hurry through its objectives.

content.headline: How Rockstar built Grand Theft Auto VI’s detailed version of Florida
content.shortHeadline: Inside Rockstar’s research for Grand Theft Auto VI
content.standfirst: Rockstar developers describe years of research that helped build Vice City and virtual Florida, from its neighbourhoods to small everyday details. The feature also shows how fieldwork informs the setting before the game’s story and characters take shape.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto VI, Rockstar’s forthcoming game.

sources.originalTitle: How years of research built Grand Theft Auto VI’s obsessively detailed world

segments.body: Rockstar developers began travelling to Miami in 2015 to research the setting for Grand Theft Auto VI. Rob Nelson says the team first immersed itself in the place and its history, considering the locations and contrasts they wanted players to experience before deciding what story to tell there.

segments.title: A world built from observation
segments.body: The game’s fictional Florida, Leonida, includes Vice City and is designed with detail at scales from architecture and geography to clothes, street art and the contents of a fridge. Nelson demonstrates small character behaviours, while describing a production involving almost 5,000 people.

The developers’ research included nightclubs, police ridealongs and the Florida Keys. Nelson says Rockstar’s team still sees much to explore in the United States, and calls the studio an outsider to the version of America it is portraying.

content.headline: Titanium Court’s strangest moments make it one of the year’s most memorable
content.shortHeadline: Titanium Court is weird, surprising and hard to forget
content.standfirst: AP Thomson’s game combines lo-fi fairies, strategy and optional songs in a world that delights in unpredictability. The feature argues that its strange turns are not a distraction from the experience but the reason to play.

image.caption: A scene from Titanium Court.

sources.originalTitle: Why the weirdest game of 2026 is also one of my favourites

segments.body: Titanium Court begins as a tile-matching strategy game in which the player leads fairy armies. It soon veers into unexpected encounters, including an optional song that replaces a boss fight with an extended, surreal performance by the game’s developer, AP Thomson.

segments.title: A game that resists explanation
segments.body: Thomson says he learned guitar to make music for the game and workshopped songs at open-mic nights. The feature describes a project that gathers fairy politics, Shakespearean echoes, lo-fi art and ideas that seem to emerge from the developer’s wide-ranging interests.

The article argues that discovery is the game’s central pleasure: its scenes can be so specific that players may wonder whether anyone else will encounter the same combination. Thomson says even his partner found a scene he did not remember writing.

content.headline: After decades playing games, GamesMaster’s Dominik Diamond is in one
