content.shortHeadline: Dominik Diamond makes his video-game debut after 50 years of play
content.standfirst: The former GamesMaster presenter voices the hero of an independent survival-horror game made by a small team in Nova Scotia. He writes about the strangeness of hearing his voice in the game—and showing it to his children.

image.caption: Draga, the protagonist of Black Tides Draga’s Wake.

sources.originalTitle: After 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in one

segments.body: Dominik Diamond, who presented GamesMaster, was asked to voice Draga, the sailor hero of Black Tides Draga’s Wake. The survival-horror game follows a crew on a decaying steamship after a heist goes wrong, with Draga infected by an ancient god.

segments.title: Finding the character’s voice
segments.body: Diamond says his first recordings sounded wrong to him, so he lowered his voice and stopped trying to act so hard. He describes the improvised fight noises as an especially odd part of the work, made in a garage in rural Nova Scotia while the developer directed him.

The game is being made by a team working in different places and in their spare time. Diamond says that playing the result has made him think differently about voice acting and about the apparent lack of agency of game characters. His favourite moment was showing the game to his children before revealing he was in it.

content.headline: Euclid’s first major release maps more than 900m galaxies
content.shortHeadline: Euclid maps more than 900m galaxies
content.standfirst: The European space telescope has also identified about 15,000 likely cases of strong gravitational lensing. Researchers hope these distorted images of distant galaxies can help test ideas about dark matter.

image.caption: A detail of the universe captured by the Euclid mission.

sources.originalTitle: European survey reveals 900m galaxies – and possibly secrets of ‘dark universe’

segments.body: The European Space Agency’s Euclid mission has released its first major tranche of data, capturing more than 900m galaxies and over 60m possible quasars. The survey covers about 14% of the sky Euclid is expected to map as it builds a three-dimensional picture of the universe.

segments.title: A clue in distorted light
segments.body: The data includes about 15,000 probable examples of strong gravitational lensing, in which the gravity of a foreground galaxy bends and magnifies light from a more distant one. Researchers say the effect is shaped by dark matter, so studying how it is distributed may help distinguish between theories of what the substance is.

perspectives.body: Stephen Serjeant of the Open University says lensing could offer a route to a breakthrough in understanding dark matter, but stresses that it is a possibility, not a certainty.

segments.body: The mission is expected to find around 170,000 strong-lensing cases by its end, compared with about 1,000 previously known to experts, according to the report. A further data release is expected next summer, including work on the distribution of galaxies and weaker lensing effects.

content.headline: Tiny medical robots show promise for targeted drug delivery
content.shortHeadline: Tiny robots could deliver drugs more precisely
content.standfirst: Early research ranges from swallowable cameras already used in the NHS to experimental devices tested in animals and models. The work is promising, but blood-vessel robots remain years from patient use.

image.caption: Illustration accompanying reporting on a medical micro-robot designed to deliver drugs in the gut.

sources.originalTitle: The astonishing micro-robots you swallow that spot cancer and might help treat it

segments.body: Swallowable camera capsules are already used to investigate gut problems, and some can be steered inside the stomach with magnets. More ambitious medical micro-robots are still experimental: researchers are developing devices intended to carry drugs to specific sites in the body, potentially reducing the amount needed elsewhere.

segments.title: What has been tested
segments.body: A team in Beijing reported using a 6.5mm magnetic device to deliver insulin to the lower intestine of pigs. Separately, researchers at ETH Zürich have guided a 2mm robot through a pig’s bloodstream; in a silicone model of brain circulation, it delivered a drug that dissolved a clot. These are animal and model tests, not demonstrations of treatment in people.

perspectives.body: Roboticist Bradley Nelson of ETH Zürich says targeting a drug to a specific location could reduce the dose needed and help address toxicity. That potential has yet to be established in clinical use.

segments.body: Other groups are developing microscopic particles and swarms, including devices that heated and destroyed tumours in mice. The article says robots small enough to travel through human blood vessels are probably at least a decade from patient use, underlining how far these approaches remain from routine medicine.

content.headline: Government report classifies sugars in smoothies as free sugars
content.shortHeadline: Blending fruit makes its sugars count as free sugars
content.standfirst: A UK advisory report says blending, crushing or juicing fruit releases sugars from plant cells, while chopping generally does not. The health implications and how the sugars affect blood glucose remain debated.

sources.originalTitle: Why smoothies are worse for you than raw fruit – and the healthier alternatives

segments.body: The UK government’s Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition says sugars in fruit become “free sugars” when the fruit is blended, crushed, pressed or sieved, as in smoothies and juices. Chopping, dicing or grating fruit leaves its cellular structure largely intact and does not release significant free sugars, according to the report.

segments.title: What that means for diets
segments.body: Free sugars include added sugars as well as sugars released from plant cells. Health guidance recommends limiting them, partly because studies link higher consumption of added free sugars with excess weight and tooth decay in children. But the report does not settle why released sugars may be harmful, and a small trial cited in the coverage found similar blood-sugar rises after whole fruit and smoothies containing the same amount of sugar.

perspectives.body: Dietitian Carrie Ruxton argues that chewing whole fruit slows consumption and that its fibre and other nutrients can help people feel full. The report’s classification is not, by itself, a claim that smoothies have no nutritional value.

segments.body: Juice loses some of the fruit’s fibre and can make it easier to consume a large amount quickly, food scientist Ciaran Forde says. The article notes that smoothies and juices need not be excluded altogether: NHS guidance allows them to count as one of the recommended five daily portions of fruit and vegetables.

content.headline: Atrial fibrillation can go unnoticed; wearable alerts are not a diagnosis
content.shortHeadline: Watch alerts can flag an irregular heartbeat, not diagnose it
content.standfirst: Atrial fibrillation can raise the risk of stroke, but smartwatch alerts need clinical follow-up and can also cause anxiety when checks find no ongoing problem. A large UK trial is due to report in 2028.

sources.originalTitle: The overlooked sign you could develop dementia – and how your watch could spot it

segments.body: Atrial fibrillation is an irregular rhythm in which the heart’s upper chambers beat out of coordination. It can come and go, and some people have no obvious symptoms. Blood can pool in the heart during an episode and form clots, raising the risk of stroke; the condition is also associated with longer-term heart and brain harms.

segments.title: What wearable alerts can and can’t do
segments.body: Some smartwatches can flag a possible rhythm abnormality, but they cannot provide a clear diagnosis. Cardiologist Gregory Lip says detection can help people reach treatment; GP and researcher Rakesh Modi cautions that brief episodes may not have clinical significance, and that follow-up checks that find no atrial fibrillation may leave some people worried.

perspectives.body: Modi says repeated alerts can add anxiety and work for the NHS. He argues that encouraging people with palpitations to speak to a GP may be more useful than broad screening campaigns.

segments.body: A large trial is testing whether people over 70 who record their heart rhythm at home and receive treatment if atrial fibrillation is found have fewer strokes, heart problems or dementia. Results are expected in 2028; the evidence has not yet settled whether routine screening should be introduced.

content.headline: Microsoft outage disrupts services worldwide as recovery continues
content.shortHeadline: Microsoft outage disrupts services worldwide
content.standfirst: A failure affecting Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft services disrupted workplaces and public services across multiple countries. Microsoft says systems are recovering, but some users may still face access problems and delayed email.

sources.originalTitle: Microsoft outage live: millions still affected as disruption stretches beyond 18 hours
NHS, schools and police forces hit by Microsoft outage
Microsoft’s latest email outage turned into a full blown global cloud crisis
Why is the Microsoft outage lasting so long?

segments.body: A Microsoft 365 outage that began on Thursday affected Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other services, disrupting organisations and users in many countries. Reports describe impacts ranging from missed emails and delayed business orders to interruptions in communications at schools, hospitals, courts and government offices. Microsoft has said there is no evidence of malicious activity.

segments.title: Recovery is not complete
segments.body: Microsoft has reported improving service availability and reduced email queues, but warned that some users could still experience intermittent access problems or delayed delivery. The company has not yet provided a full account of the underlying cause; it says it will share more after mitigation is complete.

perspectives.body: University of Reading computer scientist James Ferryman says overloaded secure-connection servers can create a cascading failure: devices repeatedly reconnecting add pressure, so services need to be brought back gradually.

segments.title: A reminder of reliance
segments.body: The outage exposed how dependent organisations are on a small number of communication and cloud platforms. UK health services and other workplaces advised people to use phone lines for urgent matters, while the Guardian reports that some companies turned to calls, fax or other backups to keep essential work moving.

content.headline: Police watchdog warns facial-recognition errors can lead to wrongful action
content.shortHeadline: Watchdog warns of risks from police facial-recognition errors
content.standfirst: An inspection found that some officers treated retrospective facial-recognition matches as evidence without enough checks. The watchdog also raised concerns about bias, retained images and gaps in the legal framework.

sources.originalTitle: Facial recognition errors put ethnic minorities at risk of wrongful arrest, police watchdog warns

segments.body: A report by His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary warns that police may take inappropriate action against people if they rely too heavily on retrospective facial-recognition results. Inspectors found some investigators did not understand that a potential match is intelligence requiring further enquiries, not proof of identity.

segments.title: Bias and oversight concerns
segments.body: The report identifies continuing risks of inaccurate matches, including a greater likelihood of wrongly flagging people from ethnic minorities, and says poor-quality or unsuitable images can make results less reliable. Inspectors also found custody images that should have been deleted were retained, and said there is no comprehensive statutory framework governing the technology’s use.

perspectives.body: The National Police Chiefs’ Council says retrospective facial recognition can help investigate crime and supports its responsible use. The watchdog and civil-liberties critics argue that clearer rules and stronger safeguards are needed.

segments.body: Inspectors say public confidence depends on appropriate safeguards, managing bias and data-retention risks, and maintaining human judgement. The report is about retrospective searches; it does not cover live facial recognition, which is used to identify people in real time.

content.headline: NHS England removes claim that 137 trusts benefit from Palantir system
content.shortHeadline: NHS removes claim that 137 trusts benefit from Palantir system
content.standfirst: The change follows reporting that 29 trusts were not using all or most of the company’s data platform. A statistics regulator is examining NHS claims as ministers consider extending Palantir’s contract.

image.caption: Demonstrators protest Palantir’s role in the NHS.

sources.originalTitle: NHS England deletes ‘misleading’ claim 137 trusts benefiting from Palantir AI tools

segments.body: NHS England has removed a webpage listing 137 hospital trusts as live with and benefiting from Palantir’s Federated Data Platform. The change came after 29 trusts said they were not using all or most of the system, according to the Guardian’s reporting. A less detailed page now refers to early users seeing results.

segments.title: Dispute over evidence and the contract
segments.body: The Office for Statistics Regulation is examining NHS claims about the platform’s use. Critics say its benefits have been overstated, while a Labour MP quoted by the Guardian says unverified claims risk undermining trust. Campaign groups and unions oppose extending the £330m contract; Palantir says ending it would put politics above patients.

perspectives.body: Medact’s Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne says removing the webpage is welcome but argues NHS England should explain why it promoted benefits using what she calls shaky evidence.

segments.body: Ministers are weighing whether to extend the deal to 2029. Critics say the contract could instead end in 2027 using its termination-assistance provisions, but the reporting does not establish what ministers will decide. NHS England did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.

content.headline: Heat-pump buyers turn to home surveys, but experts warn against DIY sizing
content.shortHeadline: Heat-pump sizing: why a home survey matters
content.standfirst: Heat-loss estimates help determine the size of a heat pump, but a small US study found some installer calculations substantially overstated demand. Experts disagree on whether homeowner apps help or risk putting engineering work on customers.

image.caption: Installing a heat pump requires estimating how much heat a home loses.

sources.originalTitle: Heat pumps: How much heat does your home really need?

segments.body: Heat pumps need to be sized to a home’s expected heat loss. Some homeowners are using apps to estimate that figure before choosing a system, but a calculation that is too high or low can lead to an oversized or underpowered installation.

segments.title: Accuracy is the question
segments.body: Kevin Kircher of Purdue University says an unpublished study of calculations for about 75 US homes found estimates from tradespeople often overstated design heat loads by a factor of two or more. An oversized system can use more energy and cycle on and off frequently; the small study is not evidence that every installer’s calculation is inaccurate.

perspectives.body: Researcher Maurizio Sibilla argues that better installer practice and clearer evidence for customers are the answer, rather than expecting homeowners to do engineering calculations themselves.

segments.body: Homeowner-facing tools such as Heatpunk and Cool Calc can help people understand a property, but the article also notes that commercial interests may shape some tools’ recommendations. Installers caution that hidden draughts and insulation gaps can be missed without a professional survey.

content.headline: Nvidia scandal raises questions about chip exports and US oversight
content.shortHeadline: Nvidia scandal puts chip exports and oversight under scrutiny
content.standfirst: Jensen Huang’s departure has intensified scrutiny of suspected chip diversions to China and the US government’s response. Allegations about an executive’s links to Chinese intelligence remain unproven; Congress is seeking answers from Nvidia and officials.

image.caption: Nvidia’s former chief executive, Jensen Huang.

sources.originalTitle: Nvidia scandal: Howard Lutnick under pressure over alleged lack of action
How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
Democrats launch Nvidia investigation, write scathing letter on Huang’s ‘scheme’ with Trump
Bessent blames Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to block Megaspeed
Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached?

segments.body: Nvidia’s leadership crisis has brought renewed attention to US controls on advanced AI chips and a government investigation involving Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert chips to China. The allegations that Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was linked to Chinese intelligence have not been established; China has rejected them, and Nvidia’s board says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

segments.title: Questions for officials and Nvidia
segments.body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says several agencies favoured putting Megaspeed on an export-control blacklist, while the Commerce Department had authority over that decision. Lawmakers from both parties are pressing for records and testimony. Democrats have also questioned a process under which certain chip sales to China were allowed after the chips were brought to the US for inspection.

perspectives.body: Democratic lawmakers’ letter questions the administration’s handling of chip sales and whether it continued to approve transactions despite reported intelligence concerns. As the minority party, the lawmakers can request answers but cannot compel them.

segments.title: Why the company’s role matters
segments.body: Nvidia’s chips underpin much of the AI industry, and its relationships with chip buyers, cloud providers and governments have become central to its position. The Guardian’s analysis says opaque contracts and supply chains make it difficult to establish who received chips and on what terms; the full extent of any diversion and the administration’s knowledge remain unresolved.

perspectives.body: The Guardian describes Nvidia as deeply connected to AI infrastructure financing and supply. It argues that this network, not just the chips themselves, helps explain the company’s influence—and why scrutiny of its dealings could matter beyond one leadership change.

content.headline: AI chatbots sometimes point shoppers to fake or risky retail websites
content.shortHeadline: Study finds chatbots can point shoppers to risky sites
content.standfirst: A study testing three chatbots found that some shopping answers included fake, inactive or potentially misleading websites. Its authors used their own prompts, so the results do not show how often this happens in ordinary user searches.

sources.originalTitle: AI chatbots are recommending fake retail websites, study finds

segments.body: A study by brand-protection firm Podqi found that ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity sometimes surfaced what it classified as risky retail sites when asked where to buy products. Those included fake stores impersonating brands, inactive domains and sites selling knockoffs.

segments.title: What the test measured
segments.body: Podqi tested 6,795 responses to shopping questions about 151 brands, using prompts it created rather than real user conversations. It found risky sites in 4% of Gemini answers, 8% of ChatGPT answers and 15% of Perplexity answers. The study’s definition included sites merely mentioned as well as sites recommended or flagged with a warning.

perspectives.body: Podqi’s chief executive advises shoppers to verify a site independently before entering payment or personal details. Google and OpenAI said they are working to improve the reliability of shopping results.

segments.body: The study found that smaller brands appeared more exposed and that questions about regional websites were more likely to produce risky results. The findings point to a potential consumer risk, but a test designed by one company cannot establish the frequency of the problem across typical chatbot use.

content.headline: US public-sector unions negotiate safeguards as workplaces adopt AI
content.shortHeadline: Public-sector workers bargain for AI safeguards
content.standfirst: Unions in several US cities and states have won or sought rules on job displacement, worker oversight and monitoring as agencies adopt AI. The examples show concrete protections being negotiated, alongside continuing disputes about safety and control.

image.caption: Public-sector union members rally in Oakland, California.

sources.originalTitle: US public workers are fighting to protect their jobs from AI – and some are winning

segments.body: Public-sector unions are seeking protections as government agencies introduce AI and automation. In Oakland, a union’s strike vote helped secure a tentative agreement requiring the city to retrain or reassign workers displaced by AI rather than dismiss them.

segments.title: Rules on how tools are used
segments.body: In Pennsylvania, a union pushed for a state policy that includes employee input and human supervision and bars AI from being used to discipline workers. California has passed laws restricting employers’ reliance on automated systems for firing or discipline and limiting some workplace AI surveillance. These examples do not amount to a single national standard.

perspectives.body: Union leaders say contract negotiations can establish safeguards while policymakers move slowly. They are not uniformly opposed to technology: some support tools that improve transport safety, provided people retain oversight.

segments.body: The article cites a 2026 survey in which nearly 70% of state and local government agencies said they had adopted or were implementing generative AI. Workers are also concerned about monitoring systems that rank performance, track activity or inform hiring and promotion decisions.

content.headline: AI-enhanced property photos can mislead homebuyers, BBC reports
content.shortHeadline: AI-enhanced property photos risk misleading buyers
content.standfirst: Homebuyers and sellers told the BBC that altered listing photos changed rooms or removed features without clear disclosure. UK guidance allows basic enhancements but says structural changes or concealed features could mislead consumers and break the law.

image.caption: A property listing’s AI-enhanced images compared with how the home looked in person.

sources.originalTitle: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?

segments.body: Estate agents are using AI to edit property photos, from clearing clutter to changing the appearance of rooms. A buyer interviewed by the BBC said a home looked different in person, including smaller rooms and structural features absent from the online images; the listing photos had been AI-enhanced.

segments.title: Where enhancement crosses a line
segments.body: The Guild of Property Professionals has issued guidance on responsible use. Trading Standards told the BBC that basic enhancements or virtual furnishings can be used if disclosed, but changing a room’s structure or hiding features could mislead buyers and break the law. A survey cited in the report found one in five recent UK homebuyers had viewed a property whose photos were digitally enhanced to make it look better.

perspectives.body: The estate agency Howards says it has introduced a policy of labelling AI-enhanced photos and does not use AI to misrepresent a property’s fundamental features.

segments.body: A property seller told the BBC that an agent had altered images of her children’s rooms. The report shows that AI editing can affect sellers as well as prospective buyers, and that disclosure practices are not yet consistent across the examples described.

content.headline: AI-assisted animation reaches Disney+ as studios test new workflows
content.shortHeadline: Animaj brings AI-assisted animation to Disney+
content.standfirst: Animaj says its AI tools help human animators work faster on the preschool series Ozzy Fox, while retaining control of each frame. The company’s claims about productivity and quality are promotional and not independently assessed in the report.

image.caption: Ozzy Fox, the AI-assisted animated series from Animaj and Disney.

sources.originalTitle: Animaj Brings ‘Ozzy Fox’ Series to Disney Plus as It Charts a Path for AI in Animation

segments.body: Ozzy Fox, produced by animation studio Animaj with Disney, is drawn and animated by people with AI tools used to speed parts of the process. The series has appeared on YouTube and Disney Junior and is due to arrive on Disney+.

segments.title: A tool for the production pipeline
segments.body: Animaj says its workflow uses agents to interpret notes and select tools, and AI to help fill in movement between animator-drawn poses. The company says animators retain control at every frame and that the system uses in-house models with context about the show’s characters and style.

perspectives.body: Animaj argues that AI can reduce repetitive work and give storytellers more time for creative decisions. Its claims about faster production and improved quality are the company’s own.

segments.body: The report says the writers and animators involved kept their jobs, but it does not establish how widely this model will be adopted or how it will affect employment across the industry. The discussion also reflects unresolved disagreement over when AI-assisted work should be called AI-generated or labelled as “slop.”

content.headline: Nebius plans $40bn AI infrastructure expansion amid delivery delays
content.shortHeadline: Nebius plans $40bn AI buildout as projects face delays
content.standfirst: The neocloud company expects customer prepayments and loans to fund much of its planned 2027 spending. Delays at a Microsoft-linked data-centre site highlight the risks if capacity arrives late and revenues slip.

sources.originalTitle: Nebius tests the neocloud playbook with $40 billion in planned spending

segments.body: Nebius has outlined $40bn in planned spending for 2027 to expand AI computing infrastructure. It expects customer prepayments and loans secured against contracts to cover much of the investment, a model that depends on projects arriving in time to generate revenue.

segments.title: A delayed site raises questions
segments.body: A New Jersey data centre supplying Microsoft is months behind schedule. Nebius says the operator’s shift away from temporary generation accelerated the delay; the site had previously faced a fine over unpermitted gas generators and a noise-complaint lawsuit. The reporting does not establish that Microsoft has agreed to the revised delivery dates.

perspectives.body: Nebius says delays are at third-party sites it does not control and that its own data centres are coming online on time or early. Microsoft has not publicly cancelled its contract, but its stated spending was lower than expected because of third-party delays.

segments.body: Nebius reported $981m in third-quarter revenue and ended the quarter with $7.4bn in cash, but cut its 2026 revenue forecast by $200m, citing site delays. The company’s plan illustrates how customer-backed financing can amplify the consequences of construction slippage; its 2027 spending and revenue projections remain forecasts.
